strengths: The paper identifies an important weakness of video MLLMs: performance drops substantially when incorrect choices are visually or semantically similar to the correct action.

Using strong action-recognition models to mine difficult distractors is practical and more informative than random negative sampling. The comparison among random, AVION, and TIM distractors clearly demonstrates the effect of distractor quality.
The proposed system is evaluated extensively, including multiple model sizes, cumulative and leave-one-out ablations, qualitative examples, and six external video benchmarks.

The resulting models substantially improve over their LLaVA starting points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, including under the AVION-to-TIM distribution shift. The manuscript also supplies useful implementation details, prompts, licensing information, and training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The claimed state-of-the-art comparison on standard EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action classification is not valid as presented. LLaVAction reranks TIM's top-20 candidates, whereas the cited baselines predict over the full action vocabulary. The benchmark construction elsewhere explicitly inserts the ground-truth answer into the candidate set; it is unclear whether the same oracle insertion occurs in Table 4. Either interpretation makes the comparison materially different from ordinary top-1 classification, yet the paper labels the result SOTA.

The main gains do not establish that the proposed architectural techniques are responsible for the improvement. The largest factor is supervised fine-tuning directly on the target multiple-choice format using AVION hard negatives. There are no comparably fine-tuned LLaVA baselines, simple classifier/reranker controls, or parameter- and data-matched alternatives that isolate the value of the action token and auxiliary tasks.

The ablation evidence is internally weak. Although the cumulative experiment attributes a 3.9-point gain to vision supervision, removing vision supervision from the full model costs only 0.3 points. GPT-4o distillation similarly contributes only 0.2 points in the leave-one-out study. Interactions are not analyzed, and no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are reported, despite many claimed gains being below two points.

EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA is fundamentally a model-conditioned reranking benchmark: all negatives reflect confusions of a particular action classifier, and the correct answer is guaranteed among only five choices. This narrows what its accuracy demonstrates and creates possible benchmark-specific shortcuts. Human validation of distractor correctness and ambiguity, robustness to additional negative generators, and analysis of text-only or shuffled-video baselines are missing.

The comparison against GPT-4o contrasts a zero-shot general model with a model extensively trained on 530K pairs derived from the target dataset. It demonstrates successful specialization but does not by itself support a general superiority claim. GPT-4o is also evaluated with only eight frames, while the strongest proposed result uses sixteen frames and test-time action memory.

Generalization evidence is modest: improvements over LLaVA-Video-7B are mostly 0.4–2.5 points, NextQA decreases, and VideoMME action recognition and action reasoning both decline. These results are presented without uncertainty and do not convincingly establish broadly improved action understanding.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations and ethical-impact discussion, including possible privacy concerns inherited from egocentric video and the consequences of model-generated annotations. Overall, the benchmark idea is useful, but the unfair SOTA comparison and insufficiently controlled evaluation undermine central claims at a top-tier acceptance bar.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: fine-grained action understanding remains a genuine weakness of multimodal video models.
Using strong action-recognition models to mine difficult distractors is intuitive, scalable, and substantially more informative than random negative sampling.
The empirical study is broad, covering multiple LLaVA-family backbones, EPIC-KITCHENS-100, several auxiliary objectives, and seven external video benchmarks.

The authors disclose several important qualifications, including IID versus OOD distractor settings, the weaker results with official action keys, and the fact that the external-benchmark results are not state of the art.
The main EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA improvement is large, and the comparison between random, AVION-derived, and TIM-derived negatives provides useful evidence for the value of hard-negative training.
weaknesses: The proposed benchmark lacks essential validity controls. There is no text-only baseline, shuffled-video test, or human study of option ambiguity. Because the correct answer is the narration associated with the clip while distractor narrations are sampled from other clips, language artifacts, annotation style, or differing specificity may make questions solvable without recognizing the action.

The claimed state-of-the-art EPIC-KITCHENS-100 result is not directly comparable to the listed action classifiers. LLaVAction reranks TIM's top-20 predictions, apparently with the ground-truth answer inserted when absent, and therefore uses TIM as an additional proposal model plus a constrained candidate set. Comparing this cascade against standalone classifiers, including TIM itself, overstates the contribution.

Most purported methodological novelty is a collection of familiar techniques—hard-negative training, auxiliary classification, temporal localization, distillation, direct-prediction multitasking, and action-history conditioning—rather than a clear new technical insight. The dominant gain appears to come from task-specific fine-tuning with mined negatives.

The ablations do not cleanly support the component claims. In the leave-one-out study, removing vision supervision, GPT-4o distillation, or direct prediction changes accuracy by only 0.3, 0.2, and 0.6 points, respectively; this contrasts with the much larger gains attributed to them in the order-dependent cumulative ablation. Interactions, variance, and training-order effects are not analyzed.

No uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance tests are reported. This is especially problematic for the external benchmarks, where most gains are only 0.4–2.5 points, NextQA decreases, and several category-level results regress.

The external-benchmark comparison does not isolate the proposed techniques from additional training data and compute: LLaVAction is trained with EPIC-KITCHENS-derived data and replay data, while it is compared against a released baseline rather than a compute- and data-matched control. Consequently, the claimed generalization is weakly identified.

Benchmark construction depends on one particular model, TIM. Evaluation against AVION-generated, alternative-model-generated, human-curated, or cross-domain hard negatives is missing, so robustness beyond TIM's error distribution is unclear.

The benchmark is derived from an existing validation split and the principal action-recognition claim is also reported only on that validation split. There is no held-out challenge-test evaluation, limiting confidence in the headline result.

The prior-action test-time augmentation is potentially vulnerable to sequential error propagation, but the paper provides no oracle-versus-predicted-history comparison, sequence-level analysis, or computational accounting.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite partial hyperparameter reporting: the exact task-mixture ratios, sampling details, loss weights, decoding configuration, seeds, and data-generation artifacts are not sufficiently specified. Training also requires 32 GH200 GPUs, making independent verification unusually difficult.

Overall, the paper contains useful engineering observations, but the missing benchmark controls, questionable comparability of the SOTA claim, and inadequately isolated generalization evidence are substantial enough that it is not competitive at a top-tier venue in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: fine-grained action recognition remains difficult for general-purpose video MLLMs despite their strong performance on conventional multiple-choice benchmarks.

EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA is a useful benchmark contribution. Generating hard distractors from specialist action-recognition models produces a substantially more discriminative evaluation than random choices; for example, GPT-4o falls from 87.6% with random distractors to 52.2% with TIM distractors.

The empirical improvements on the proposed benchmark are large and consistent across model sizes and families. LLaVAction raises LLaVA-Video-7B from roughly 35% zero-shot accuracy to 73.4% in the AVION-to-TIM OOD setting, and the 0.5B and OneVision variants also improve substantially.

Using AVION-generated negatives for training and TIM-generated negatives for evaluation is a thoughtful control that reduces direct overfitting to the benchmark's distractor generator. The additional IID result is clearly identified as such.
The study includes incremental and leave-one-out ablations, comparisons of 8 versus 16 frames, official-key versus narration representations, and evaluations on six established video benchmarks.

The method achieves a modest improvement over specialist action-recognition systems on the original EPIC-KITCHENS-100 validation protocol when reranking TIM candidates, while the broader benchmark results suggest that the training generally preserves rather than catastrophically damages existing video capabilities.
The paper is clearly motivated and generally well presented, with informative qualitative examples and useful discussion of why compressed action labels can be problematic for language-based models.
weaknesses: The proposed benchmark assumes exactly one valid answer but provides no human ambiguity audit or inter-annotator validation. Narrations sampled from closely related predicted classes can be semantically equivalent or simultaneously compatible with a short clip, making some apparent errors difficult to interpret.

The headline EPIC-KITCHENS-100 result is not standalone action classification: LLaVAction reranks TIM's top-20 predictions. Consequently, the 58.3% versus TIM's 56.4% comparison demonstrates a useful refinement stage but supports a narrower SOTA claim than the presentation initially suggests. Results are also limited to the validation set rather than the official test set.

The comparison to GPT-4o is not fully matched: GPT-4o is evaluated zero-shot with eight sampled frames, whereas LLaVAction receives extensive in-domain supervision, including adversarial multiple-choice examples. The 21-point headline gap therefore should not be interpreted as a general superiority result.

Much of the gain comes from task-specific MQA fine-tuning with hard negatives rather than the individually novel architectural or auxiliary components. In the leave-one-out study, vision supervision, GPT-4o distillation, and direct prediction contribute only 0.3, 0.2, and 0.6 points, respectively; this also differs considerably from their larger incremental gains, indicating strong order or interaction effects that are not analyzed.

Evidence for broad action-understanding generalization is modest. Improvements over LLaVA-Video-7B range from 0.4 to 2.5 points on five external benchmarks, NextQA drops by 0.4, and the VideoMME action-recognition and action-reasoning subcategories both decline. Several gains may be within evaluation variance, but no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a resource-intensive study: the manuscript does not report loss weights and sampling ratios across all auxiliary datasets, random seeds, run-to-run variance, or sufficiently precise benchmark-construction artifacts. The displayed code-and-model availability statement also lacks a usable URL in the submitted PDF.

The prior-action mechanism is trained with ground-truth history but tested with model-generated history, and its gain is only about 0.5–0.7 points. Exposure bias and error accumulation are not studied.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: evaluating and improving fine-grained action understanding in video MLLMs, where randomly sampled multiple-choice distractors can substantially overestimate capability.

The specialist-generated hard-negative benchmark is practically useful and clearly more challenging than random-choice evaluation; the large drops observed across GPT-4o and several open models support this motivation.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering three model sizes, EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, established action-recognition datasets, 13 general video-MLLM benchmarks, multiple domains, and both additive and leave-one-out ablations.
The proposed training recipe produces large gains over the underlying LLaVA-Video model, while replaying general instruction data largely preserves performance on broader video benchmarks.
Implementation information—including training data scale, optimization settings, frame counts, compute, prompts, licenses, and promised release of models/data/code—supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The strongest action-recognition results are produced by a two-stage ensemble that uses a strong task-specific recognizer such as TIM, Multi-modal VideoMAE, or SlowFast to construct the candidate set. Comparing this system against standalone specialist models and describing the result as LLaV Action achieving SOTA obscures the contribution of the first-stage model. Candidate recall/oracle accuracy, end-to-end baselines using the same first stage, and compute-matched comparisons are needed.

Benchmark validity is insufficiently established. Correct and incorrect options are sampled differently, no text-only or shuffled-video baseline tests whether narration artifacts permit shortcut solving, and there is no human audit or inter-annotator analysis of whether the fine-grained choices are visually distinguishable and uniquely correct. The paper itself shows that action labels can be ambiguous.

Calling AVION-generated training choices and TIM-generated test choices an OOD setting is not well justified: both use the same EPIC-KITCHENS task, label space, and underlying split protocol. The supporting statistics are unclear—the reported confidence interval is inconsistent with the stated mean and standard deviation, the null hypothesis behind the p-value and Cohen's d is unspecified, and reduced accuracy when increasing K is confounded by the intrinsically harder test task rather than demonstrating overfitting.

The architectural novelty is limited: the action token is essentially an auxiliary supervised classification token, while the two-stage method is specialist-guided reranking and hard-negative training is established. Moreover, the leave-one-out ablation attributes only 0.5 points to the action token, considerably weaker than the 3.9-point sequential additive gain emphasized in the main text.

The attention analysis does not substantiate the claimed mechanism. Comparing attention to one action token against attention to each of many visual tokens is inherently scale-confounded, raw attention is not reliable evidence of information use, and the action token can attend to preceding system tokens as well as visual tokens.

Most gains on the 13 general MLLM benchmarks are small, several benchmarks regress, and no multi-seed variance or significance analysis is reported. Thus the broad generalization claim is stronger than the evidence.
The ethics discussion is cursory. Fine-grained human-action recognition has privacy and surveillance implications that are not addressed, even if the training datasets contain routine activities.

strengths: The specialist-model-based hard-negative construction exposes weaknesses that random multiple-choice distractors conceal; the large performance drops in Table 1 support the motivation.
The study covers several model scales and base architectures, four action datasets, and numerous general video-MLLM benchmarks.
Both additive and leave-one-out ablations are provided, and they indicate that hard-distractor training is the largest contributor to performance.
The two-stage candidate-reranking pipeline is computationally practical compared with exhaustive scoring over roughly 4,000 actions.
weaknesses: The core ideas are incremental: hard-negative mining, an auxiliary classification token, and specialist-generated candidate reranking are established techniques. Their combination is useful, but the paper does not establish substantial methodological novelty.

The main action-recognition results depend on a dataset-specific specialist model to generate candidates. Consequently, LLaVAction is effectively part of an ensemble, and comparisons against standalone recognition models do not isolate its contribution. Candidate recall, oracle upper bounds, and results using identical candidate generators for all competing rerankers are insufficiently reported.

The headline claim of a 21-point improvement over GPT-4o is not a controlled comparison: GPT-4o is evaluated with eight frames, whereas the result producing the stated margin uses sixteen. At eight frames, the reported improvement is about 19 points. Prompt sensitivity and closed-model evaluation variance are also unexamined.

EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA lacks essential benchmark validation. There is no human study, ambiguity audit, inter-annotator agreement, contamination analysis, or demonstration that sampled narrations yield one uniquely correct answer. Raw narrations and specialist error patterns may introduce exploitable language or class biases.

Generalization evidence is weaker than claimed. Most external action-dataset results require new dataset-specific specialists and finetuning; Meccano is compared only against SlowFast, and the general MLLM benchmark gains are often very small, lack uncertainty estimates, and include regressions on several action-focused categories.

The action-token evidence is inconclusive: its leave-one-out contribution is only 0.5 points, loss weights are unspecified, and the attention comparison between one aggregate action token and each of many visual tokens is not meaningful. The claim that the action token exclusively attends to visual tokens is inconsistent with the stated causal sequence, which also permits attention to preceding system-text tokens.
No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests are given for the main results, making the many sub-point benchmark gains difficult to distinguish from evaluation or training noise.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for external-dataset finetuning, candidate construction, decoding and answer parsing. The paper states that code and models are available, but the manuscript contains no usable anonymized resource link.
The ethics discussion is cursory: public availability does not eliminate privacy, surveillance, licensing, or downstream behavior-monitoring concerns associated with egocentric human-activity data.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: whether video MLLMs can discriminate fine-grained actions rather than succeed through coarse semantic matching.

EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA is a useful benchmark contribution. Mining distractors from strong action-recognition models produces substantially harder and more realistic alternatives than random sampling, exposing large drops for GPT-4o and existing open models.

The main empirical gains are large and convincing: LLaVAction improves its LLaVA-Video-7B base from 34.8% to 74.1% in the AVION-to-TIM setting and exceeds GPT-4o by roughly 21 points on the proposed benchmark.

The evaluation is unusually broad, spanning multiple base-model sizes, EPIC-KITCHENS, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen, MECCANO, Animal Kingdom, and 13 general video-MLLM benchmarks. Results suggest that specialization does not substantially sacrifice general video understanding.

The paper includes useful additive and leave-one-out ablations. These identify hard-distractor training as the largest contributor while providing evidence that temporal supervision, direct prediction, and the action token offer complementary benefits.

The structured-prediction analysis addresses a genuine practical issue for MLLMs with large label spaces, and the reported efficiency advantage over exhaustive likelihood scoring is substantial. Training details, prompts, licensing information, and compute requirements are also documented.
weaknesses: The claimed out-of-distribution characterization is overstated. AVION and TIM operate on the same dataset and label space, have 65% top-1 agreement, and generate correlated errors. The observation that performance decreases as K increases does not establish overfitting because the test task simultaneously becomes harder. The reported JSD confidence interval also appears inconsistent with its stated mean.

The strongest action-recognition results rely on a two-stage ensemble whose first stage is an external specialist model. Consequently, comparisons against standalone specialist models do not isolate LLaVAction's capability. Candidate recall, oracle upper bounds, and the incremental gain over the complete first-stage model should be reported consistently for every transfer dataset.

Much of the gain comes from task-specific hard-negative data rather than the architectural contribution. In the leave-one-out ablation, removing the action token reduces accuracy by only 0.5 points, while the larger additive gain is sensitive to component ordering. Thus, the architectural novelty and its practical importance are modest.

The narration-based 63.2% EPIC-KITCHENS result is difficult to compare directly with conventional label-based action recognition because narrations provide richer, less standardized descriptions. The 58.3% label-based result is the appropriate SOTA comparison, and the distinction should be emphasized more carefully.

Several broad generalization claims rest on small changes without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. On the 13 general benchmarks, many improvements are below one point and some action-related categories degrade; the MECCANO result is presented with particularly little experimental detail.

The attention analysis is suggestive rather than mechanistic: larger raw attention values do not establish greater visual reliance, and comparing a single aggregated action token with individual visual tokens is not a controlled causal test.

The ethics discussion is too cursory. Public availability and routine activities do not eliminate privacy, consent, surveillance, or behavioral-monitoring risks associated with egocentric human-action recognition. These limitations and possible misuse should be acknowledged.
